title: Follow Balaam in the highlands of Moab

plains.name: Plains of Moab
plains.text: The low plain east of the Jordan, across from Jericho, where Israel camped before crossing into Canaan (Numbers 22:1). Numbers 33:49 says the camp stretched from Beth Jeshimoth to Abel Shittim. The exact limits of the camp are not known.

jericho.name: Jericho
jericho.text: The oasis city west of the Jordan, identified with Tell es-Sultan. Numbers repeatedly locates Israel's camp as across the Jordan from Jericho (Numbers 22:1).

pisgah.name: Pisgah
pisgah.text: Balak took Balaam to the field of Zophim on the top of Pisgah for the second oracle (Numbers 23:14). Deuteronomy 34:1 links Pisgah with Mount Nebo, so it is usually placed on the Nebo ridge. The exact viewing point cannot be fixed.

arnon.name: Arnon
arnon.text: Balak went out to meet Balaam at a Moabite town on the Arnon border (Numbers 22:36). The Arnon is the deep canyon now called Wadi Mujib. Which town Numbers means is uncertain.

madaba.name: Madaba
madaba.text: Modern town in Jordan on the plateau above the plains of Moab, shown for orientation.

jerusalem.name: Jerusalem
jerusalem.text: Shown for orientation west of the Jordan.

chapters.title: Israel camps across from Jericho
chapters.html:
Near the end of the wilderness years, Israel camped on the plains of Moab, on the east side of the Jordan across from Jericho. The camp lay below the Moabite highlands.

Balak son of Zippor, king of Moab, had heard what Israel did to the Amorites. Moab was terrified of so many people, and the Moabites turned to the elders of Midian for help.
facts: The plains of Moab lie in the Jordan Valley well below sea level, just north of the Dead Sea, the lowest land surface on earth.
The Mesha Stele, found at Dhiban in 1868, is the longest known inscription in the Moabite language. It dates to the ninth century BC, long after Balak.

chapters.title: Balak sends for Balaam
chapters.html:
Balak sent messengers to Balaam son of Beor at Pethor, near the River, asking him to come and curse Israel. God told Balaam not to go. A second, more honored delegation came, and God let him go, but only to speak what God told him.

On the road, Balaam's donkey saw the angel of the Lord blocking the way. Balak met Balaam at a town on the Arnon border.
quote: What have I done to you to make you beat me these three times?
facts: The River in Numbers 22:5 usually means the Euphrates, and Pethor is often placed in northern Mesopotamia, far to the northeast of this map. The identification is debated.
The Arnon canyon, today's Wadi Mujib, cuts deep into the plateau and served as Moab's northern border (Numbers 21:13).

chapters.title: Blessings from the heights
chapters.html:
Balak took Balaam to three high places where he could see Israel's camp: Bamoth Baal, the field of Zophim on the top of Pisgah, and the top of Peor. At each one Balak built seven altars and offered sacrifices.

Each time, Balaam blessed Israel instead of cursing it. Balak's anger grew, and Balaam went home after delivering his final oracles.
quote: God is not human, that he should lie, not a human being, that he should change his mind.
facts: A plaster inscription found at Tell Deir Alla in the Jordan Valley, from about the eighth century BC, names a seer called Balaam son of Beor.
Bamoth Baal means "high places of Baal." Its location, like that of Peor, is uncertain.

chapters.title: The trap at Peor
chapters.html:
While Israel stayed at Shittim, the men began sexual immorality with Moabite women and joined in worshiping the Baal of Peor. A plague struck the camp until Phinehas the priest acted, and twenty-four thousand people died.

Numbers 31:16 later says the women acted on Balaam's advice. Balaam was killed with the kings of Midian when Israel went to war against Midian (Numbers 31:8).
facts: Shittim means "acacia trees." Joshua later sent the two spies to Jericho from Shittim (Joshua 2:1).
The New Testament also remembers Balaam's advice to Balak as a warning (Revelation 2:14).
